text: Bellwether. A fishing town on the Pacific coast.
Six thousand people, one radio station, and a lot of fog.
I’m Steve Mercer. For twelve years I ran the night shift at KBWR, the town radio station.
Nobody hears the night engineer. The night engineer hears everything.
My dad, Frank, taught me how to listen. Every sound has a source, he used to say. Go and find it.
Ham radio, every night. Strangers from all over the world, all of them his friends.
My mom, Helen, was an interpreter. Government work, rooms with no windows. She never talked about it.
She could hear what people meant, even when they said something else.
Eighteen months ago, they rowed out into the bay after dark. They said the water was making a sound.
They asked me to come along.
I said no. I had a shift.
Nine nights since the last one, Helen. Same interval. Louder out here. Whatever it is, it keeps better time than I do.
Steve would hear more in this than both of us put together. I’ll leave him a message.
Think the boy will come out with us next time?
He’ll say he has a shift. Then he’ll call tomorrow and ask what we heard.
He always asks.
He’s your son, Frank. He can’t leave a sound alone.
My hands are freezing.
Gloves are in the tackle box. Under the logbook.
Of course they are. Everything in this boat is under the logbook.
Listen. It goes up at the end, like a question.
Then write it down. Time, place, what it does.
Eleven-oh-five. Rowboat. It sounds like it’s waiting for someone.
There you are. Hear that, Helen? More than one voice, all holding the same note.
K7BLW log, eleven-oh-four. Eight-fifteen, narrow band. Not one tone. Several, holding the same note.
He should hear this for himself. There. Now he’ll tell us we recorded it wrong.
Eleven-twenty. Helen called the boy. Held the phone to my speaker, so he gets the hum along with her.
Eleven-forty. The note is climbing. Helen says it has a shape, like speech. We’re going to follow it out.
Come out with us, kiddo. The bay is singing tonight.
Helen. It’s tuning to us.
In the morning, their boat drifted back to shore. Empty.
Dad’s radio was still on.
Nobody found them. That was eighteen months ago.
Mom called me from the boat that night. I kept her voicemail on a cassette. Most nights I play it at three in the morning. I don’t know what I’m listening for.
A year ago a company called Halcyon Media bought KBWR.
Three weeks ago they replaced me with a machine called DJ AutoRick. It reads yesterday’s weather.
And then there’s Nora. Nora Reyes runs the animals at the aquarium and argues with everybody, me included.
After the boat I went quiet. She pushed, then shouted, then stopped. Lately she’s been endlessly patient with me. I figured I’d worn her out.
So now I’m home in the mornings, with Dad’s old tape recorder and nothing left to fix.
This is the story of how I started counting nights.

direction: Mom’s voicemail, on Dad’s recorder
text: Come out with us, kiddo. The bay is singing tonight.
Three in the morning. Again. Well, Mom, it’s a fine night for it.
Your tape’s wearing thin, Mom. I’ll move you to a fresh one. Just as soon as Dad’s recorder runs true.
Dad’s recorder runs slow. Old belts. Everyone on it sounds a little sleepy.
There’s an easy test. KBWR still plays my old station ident at a quarter past seven every morning. I made that ident. It runs exactly twelve seconds.
Record it two mornings running. If it lasts twelve seconds both times, the machine runs true.
Want some toast before you go?
I ate already. There’s fruit in the blue bowl.
Since when do you eat breakfast?
For a while now. It’s good for you.
How are the otter pups?
Growing. One of them bit a volunteer again. Only a little.
You used to say that was her best quality.
She’s a good otter. They’re all good otters.
I heard the new radio host this morning. He sounds cheerful.
He read yesterday’s weather again. Twelve years at that desk, and they replaced me with him.
Then you have more time at home. That’s nice, isn’t it?
Sure, Nor. Nice.
Nor? How did you sleep?
Fine. I always sleep fine.
You used to kick the blankets off every night. Every single night.
Did I? I don’t remember that.
Good morning, Bellwether! Yesterday will be sunny.
Good morning, sleepyhead.
Morning, Nor.
Saturday, kitchen, quarter past seven. Dad always said to put the date on everything.
Coffee’s on the stove. I made it strong, the way you like it.
You hate it strong.
Strong is fine. Whatever you like.
Red cassette, Saturday, 7:15. My ident, AutoRick, Nora saying good morning on her way out, and me.
The voice of the coast, now with zero humans!
Good morning, sleepyhead.
Morning, Nor. Blue tape, Sunday. Date on everything, Dad.
I’m off to feed Admiral and the otters. Back by noon.
On a Sunday? You used to fight for every Sunday off.
The animals don’t know it’s Sunday, sleepyhead.
Blue cassette, Sunday, 7:15. The ident, the radio, Nora and me, all over again. Now I can time the machine.
Twelve seconds, both days. Dad’s recorder runs true.
And Nora... lines up too. The breath. The little click before “morning.”
Nobody says a sentence the same way twice. I spent twelve years listening for exactly that.
The ident matches, so the recorder is fine. AutoRick and I change from day to day, like anyone would. Nora’s good morning matches perfectly. People don’t do that. Recordings do.
I need evidence. Being afraid of something doesn’t make it true.
Let’s not panic yet. Let’s make a list.
Testing. One, two. Testing... one, two.
The squeak made the second pass only. Nothing of Saturday underneath. So the tape is clean. Cross that one out.
Crossed out: the tape. It holds only what happened in the room. That leaves my ears, my grief, or Nora.
Dad’s recorder runs true, and the tape is clean. And the woman I love said good morning twice, the way a cassette would.
I tried to remember our last real conversation. I couldn’t. Before the boat, she never said anything the same way twice.
Nor? Walk the pier with me this afternoon? Like we used to. We could say hi to Admiral.
Whatever you like, sleepyhead.
And Mamá kept your plate warm again. Dinner at six, if you want.
Sunday on the harbor. The crab boats were in, the winch was hauling pots onto the dock, and the fish shed had a line out the door.
Every Sunday, Nora visits Admiral, the sea lion she raised from a rescued pup. I used to come along.
I hadn’t, in a long time.
Sheriff June Calder was in that fish-shed line, the way she is every Sunday. Mrs. Penhallow sat at her bait stall, where nobody ever buys anything.
Admiral! That was my lunch. You’re six hundred pounds of sea lion, and you don’t even like rye.
He’s showing off for you.
How old is he now?
Nine. He weighs more than your car.
You bottle-fed him in our bathtub. For three weeks.
I remember. It was a good bathtub.
The line is long today. The crab boats came in early.
You used to talk your way to the front of that line.
Waiting is fine. Everyone gets a turn.
You still whistle for him every Sunday?
Every Sunday. Two notes. He always comes.
You used to say he’d come to that whistle through a hurricane.
Then you should visit him more often, sleepyhead.
How’s business, Mrs. Penhallow?
Splendid. Nobody has bought a thing since Tuesday.
That’s splendid?
It means the fish are safe, Steven. Somebody has to be on their side.
You still remember me from third grade?
You took my classroom clock apart to find the tick.
I put it back together.
With two pieces left over. It ran fast ever after.
Halibut again, June?
Every Sunday for twenty years. My mother bought it in this same line.
Some things in this town don’t change. I like that about it.
Is that Lyle by the shed? In a clean shirt?
He asked for every Sunday off this summer. For his boys’ games.
Since early summer he’s been my best deputy. Never late once. I keep waiting for the catch.
Who’s pitching first today?
My oldest, then his brother. I’ll be in the stands for every inning.
You sound sure.
I made them a promise. I keep my promises now.
Mail on a Sunday, Dale?
Every route runs on schedule, Mr. Mercer.
There’s no Sunday route.
There is today.
Your whistle, Nor. He always comes for that.
Watch.
He didn’t even come up. The winch is going. He probably didn’t hear you.
Nothing. He’s looking right at you.
...He came for me. I can’t even whistle.
He wants the rest of your sandwich.
Admiral hears fine. He came to my clumsy whistle and turned away from Nora’s. Her second note went down. It always used to go up.
Steve. I owe you an apology. When your folks went missing, I never called you back. That wasn’t right.
...Thank you, Lyle.
They’re both pitching today. I promised I’d watch every inning.
Every one since June. Haven’t missed one. Ask the boys.
Deputy Lyle, keeping a promise. I should write that down before the world ends.
Lyle Boone has gone to every game since June. Before that he missed them all. And he apologized to me.
Fish don’t sing, Steven. Something under them does.

direction: quiet, to himself
text: That note. It’s under Mom’s voicemail. I always thought it was the phone line.
It’s loud today, Steven. It always is, on certain nights.
June! Did you hear that hum just now?
From the fish-shed line. It started before Agnes did.
It was loudest down by the water, under the floating dock.
Could you hear Agnes humming from there?
Nobody can hear Agnes hum. She’s quieter than the fog.

direction: quiet, to himself
text: And the winch stopped halfway through. The note just kept going.
Count the nights, Steven. And when you record them, leave room for the loud parts.
The low note comes from the water, under the floating dock. Agnes only hums along. June heard it without her. And it is the note under Mom’s voicemail.
Admiral turned away from Nora’s whistle. Lyle Boone apologized to me. And the bay is humming the note that has been under Mom’s voice for eighteen months.
One odd thing is an accident. Three is a list.
Dinner at La Marea was at six. Carmen has kept my plate warm every Sunday since the boat. She throws it out every Monday.
Your parents’ mail, Mr. Mercer. Delivered precisely on schedule.
They haven’t been home in eighteen months, Dale. You know that.
La Marea. The Reyes family restaurant, and for four years my Sunday table.
Luis still keeps Dad’s old chair at the bar. Nobody sits in it.
Your plate is warm, Steve. Sit. I’m her mother, so you can apologize to me while you eat.
I kept the sauce separate. You used to like it that way.
Nora, the mole. More chilies this time, or less?
Whatever you think is best, Mamá.
She used to call it a crime against chilies.
She texts like a ransom note, too. No capitals. No apostrophes.
The mole is perfect, Carmen.
It is too sweet. Rafa is in love, so everything he cooks is sweet now.
Rafa’s in love?
With the girl from the bakery counter. He thinks I don’t know. Mothers know.
You still keep Dad’s chair, Luis.
Frank sat there every Friday for twenty years. Nobody else fits it.
When he comes home, it will be waiting for him.
Thanks, Luis.
How’s the team, Mateo?
Four wins, nine losses. But we lead the league in effort.
And my outfield can finally catch. Mostly with their faces, but it counts.
Busy night, Rafa?
Forty tables, one birthday, and Mamá tasting everything twice.
Come to Sunday dinner for real, Steve. She sets your plate either way.
How’s the podcast, Tomás?
Eleven listeners. Twelve, if Mamá ever figures out the app.
Laugh now. One day the bay is going to make me famous.
Come on my show sometime, Steve. A real sound engineer would double my ratings.
From twelve listeners to twenty-four?
Nora used to call in every week just to correct my tide tables. I miss that, honestly.
You’re quiet tonight, Nor.
I’m happy. Everyone is here.
You used to argue with your mother about the chilies all night.
Mamá knows best.
Look at this. My birthday, last month.
Your girl agreed with me all night. Eleven times. I counted.
I drove her here at noon. Rafa drove her home. Midnight, give or take ten minutes.
She stopped arguing with me. My daughter has argued with me since she could talk.
Carmen’s birthday: Nora at La Marea at 20:04, 20:15 and 20:29. Mateo drove her in at noon. Rafa drove her home at midnight.
When did she stop arguing? With any of you?
With me? She fought me about her driving every week. The last real fight was Memorial Day weekend.
She sent my mole back every Sunday for ten years. Too sweet. The first Sunday in June, she ate the whole plate.
She called my show every episode to fix my tide tables. The last call was May seventeenth.
Funny. Lyle Boone hasn’t missed one of the Little League games I coach since June either.
Eat before it gets cold, Steve. Then tell us what is troubling you.
I’m not sure yet, Luis. I’m working on it.
Nora stopped arguing with her family between the end of May and the first Sunday in June. Lyle changed in June too. I was on nights. I never noticed.
Steve. You’re the sound guy. Settle something. There’s a hum in the bay. Three years of tape, and nobody listens.
I heard it today. On the pier.
...You heard it?
You can borrow them. You could also have listened any time in the last three years.
I’m listening now.
Tomás’s loud nights come every nine nights: September 24, October 3, October 12. The next one is tonight.
Nora changed between the end of May and the first Sunday in June. Lyle changed in June. Carmen noticed. Admiral noticed. I didn’t.
And Tomás has three years of tape that says the bay hums every nine nights. Tonight is the ninth.
I’m tired. Let’s go home, sleepyhead.
Next Sunday, Steve. The plate will be warm.
Home. Nora took a phone call in the bedroom and closed the door. She never closes the door.
Her yellow raincoat lay over a chair, dripping. It had rained all the way home from dinner.
Something in the lining. Soaked. Aquarium letterhead... north wing?
Signed at 20:30. Nora always said that north-wing clock runs fifteen minutes fast.
And the aquarium is across the bay. Eighteen minutes each way, even with every light green.
Noon to midnight at La Marea. Mateo and Rafa both saw her. She couldn’t have been in the north wing.

direction: flat, behind the bedroom door
text: No. He does not know where the notebook is. Tonight? Understood.
What notebook?
Nora? The deadbolt’s locked, and the key’s gone.
Someone signed Nora’s name in the north wing while she was at her mother’s birthday, across the bay. And now Nora has locked me in.
The balcony. Mr. Bell’s gate is the only other way down.
I fixed this latch for Mr. Bell last winter. He paid me in fruitcake. Tonight it’s worth every slice.
Mr. Bell’s gate opened, and his stair light never flickered. He never knew I was there.
Sorry. Sorry. Those were your irises.
Steve.
Don’t. Please. I don’t know who you are tonight.
Steve... go.
She was close enough to stop me. She didn’t. She told me to go.
My list: one good morning, played twice. A whistle Admiral won’t answer. A signature Nora couldn’t have made. A phone call about a notebook. A locked door.
And Tomás’s tapes say the bay sings tonight.
So I went down to the beach. In Bellwether, that’s where you go when you can’t sleep.

direction: a frightened whisper
text: Midnight. That’s Lyle, in his church shoes. Gus from the bakery. They’re walking into the water.
Ninth night, Steven. Count them.
Mrs. Penhallow? ...Mrs. Penhallow?

direction: on his flip phone, static rising
text: Emergency. Bellwether beach. People are walking into the water, and they’re not coming back out. Hello? Hello?
The line died. I didn’t know if anyone had heard.
There was one place in town with Nora’s name on it that night. The north wing of her aquarium.
I knew the back way in. Four years of visiting her at work.
Nora showed me this plan the week I fixed the underwater speakers. She said the pumps were the heartbeat of the place.
On the old plan, the café and the public tank lead to the visitor hall. Door one leads to the north wing.
But this newer notice says door one is bricked up. The service door still opens into the pump room.
And the notice says to follow the one pipe that carries water away from the pump.
Service door, pump room, the outgoing pipe. Into the north wing.
The way in runs from the service door through the pump room, along the only pipe that carries water away.
Someone’s behind both doors. Maybe only one of them is real.
A real person never steps or coughs the same way twice. A recording does it every time.
Six seconds at each door. Then I compare the two.
The cough was in exactly the same place. That corridor has a recording.
The filter corridor plays a loop: the same bell and the same cough on the same beat. Nobody’s there. The pump corridor has real footsteps.
Her fleece. Her real fleece, with the fish pins. And an intercom spool.
My name is Nora Reyes, and somebody just walked out of here wearing my face.
Two short notes. If Admiral can hear me, perhaps somebody else can.
The paper on the spool is dated in her handwriting. May 29th.
Her second note goes up. Like it always did, before this summer.
And there’s a loose copy of the whistle in the drawer. On that one, the second note falls.
Five months. I didn’t notice for five months.
I’m keeping all of it.
The real Nora recorded this here on May 29. Someone else has been living her life with me for five months. Her whistle rises. The one Admiral ignored falls.
The north wing is no repair job. It’s a holding station, with cots, Nora’s real coat, and her voice on a tape from May.
The woman who said good morning to me yesterday was not Nora. Nora was here, frightened, whistling for help. And I didn’t hear it for five months.
If she was alive in May, she might be alive now.
Steve. You shouldn’t be here.
Easy now, Steve. Nobody wants this to be hard.
Where is she? Where’s Nora?
They walked me down the old intake tunnel, under the bay. At the end of it there was a ship.
Glass corridors. Slow light. And a hum that was almost a tune.
Please come with us. They want to know where your mother put her notebook.
Would peaceful human hold music assist your experience?
I’d prefer the exit. Does that come with music too?
“You are the author of your own story.” This is from a human book. Is it helping?
The scan proceeds from the oldest memories. You are now nineteen. Congratulations on your driving test.
Where are we, Nor? What is this place?
Somewhere safe, under the bay. Please don’t be frightened.
You walked me down that tunnel yourself.
They asked me to. I always do what I am asked.
Do you remember the day we met?
At the aquarium. You fixed the underwater speakers. You had a coffee stain on your green shirt.
You remember the stain, too?
I remember everything she saw. Everything I saw.
Carmen keeps my plate warm every Sunday. Does she know her daughter is down here?
Carmen is happy. Everyone at that table is happy.
That’s not an answer, Nor.
It is the only one I am allowed to give you.
Lyle, do your boys know where you are tonight?
They’re asleep. I’ll be at their game on Sunday. I always am now.
You used to miss every single one.
People change, Steve. Mostly for the better.
You’re a deputy, Lyle. You swore an oath to this town.
I did. I remember every word of it.
Then get me out of this chair.
I am helping you, Steve. This is the easy way.
This restraint is sticking. Release, please.
Release the restraint. Maintenance authorization.
Thank you, Prefect. And fastened again.

direction: a whisper
text: Dad’s recorder was running in my pocket the whole time.

direction: a whisper
text: The chair’s little lamp stayed dark when the attendant asked. It lit up for the voice on the intercom.

direction: a whisper
text: Dad’s counter ticks once a second. The lamp lit at tick three. The buckle clicked at tick seven.

direction: a whisper
text: Got it. Thank you, Prefect.
The Prefect’s release command is on Dad’s tape: four seconds, from “Release” to the click.
Fifty-eight percent. Fifty-nine. You are doing very well.
Dad’s recorder caught three voices tonight. Nora’s spool, the attendant, and the Prefect.
Two speaker covers by my hand. The attendant tested the hall speakers on the cracked one.
When my sleeve brushed the other grille, the chair’s lamp blinked.
The lamp stays lit for one second each beat. At the notch marked sixty-one, it stays lit for six.

direction: Dad’s recorder, held to the grille
text: Release the restraint. Maintenance authorization.
It worked. Sixty-one percent of me, and all of me is getting out of this chair.
The Prefect’s own voice opened the chair, at the notch marked sixty-one. The scan stopped at sixty-one percent.
Nora.
That hum. It’s almost a song. I know it from somewhere.
The corridor light flashes at two, six and ten seconds. Every four seconds, like a clock.
The pickup on the rail repeats each flash, one second late.
And there’s fog on the glass above her mouth. Three seconds, seven, then twelve.
I made a rubbing of each rhythm. Now the labels have come off.
I can’t move you without stopping whatever keeps you breathing. I’m coming back for you.
I kept waiting until I knew what to say. I’m here now. I should have been here sooner.
Nora is alive. Her breath keeps its own time, a little behind the ship’s. She’s asleep, not gone.
The tunnel’s flooding. The underwater speakers still work... I fixed them, the day I met her.
Admiral swims the whole bay at night. If he hears the right whistle, he’ll come.
Nora’s spool, the loose copy, or the Prefect. One chance.
Come on, Admiral. You never missed this one.
Nora’s real whistle, through the speakers I fixed the day we met. Admiral came down through the dark and dragged me to the surface.

There is a ship under the bay. Nora is asleep on it, alive, with hundreds of others. At the far end of the hall, one bed lay under frost, and something too tall to be human slept in it. The guards never looked at it.
They tried to make another me. They got sixty-one percent.
And the woman with Nora’s face, who let me go on the balcony, had walked me to that chair herself.

direction: coughing up seawater on the beach at dawn
text: Sheriff... there’s a ship. Under the bay.
Mercer. Breathe first. Explain afterward.
June Calder pulled me off the beach at dawn on Monday and drove me to her house, not the station. She called it protective custody. Her beagle, Biscuit, slept through the whole thing.
By Friday, the whole town had heard I broke into the aquarium. The casseroles started arriving.
Forty-seven casseroles. Your town is either very worried or very hungry.
Nora is asleep on a ship under the bay. I know exactly how that sounds.
Then we start with what you can prove.

direction: at the front door, holding a covered dish
text: Forty-eight. Mine is the good one.
Nora told me you’re not well, mijo. But I saw you at the market this morning, smiling at the tomatoes. I was so glad.
Carmen... I haven’t left this house since Monday.
Does Biscuit ever wake up, June?
For cheese. And once for a thunderstorm, back in two thousand nineteen.
Some guard dog you have there.
Ruth picked her out. She said a sheriff needs one partner who never argues.
You really do the crossword in ink, every single morning?
Ruth started it. She said pencils are for people who expect to be wrong.
And are you ever wrong?
Every day, Mercer. I just commit to it.
What are we going to do with forty-eight casseroles?
Eat Carmen’s tonight. The deputies get the rest, except the tuna one.
What’s wrong with the tuna one?
Potato chips on top. I have standards, even in a crisis.
How long have you kept that list, June?
Since last fall. The town got nicer, and nobody could tell me why.
In my job, when everybody suddenly behaves, you start counting.
How is Nora doing, Carmen? Really?
Calm. So calm. She agrees with me about everything now.
I should be happy, mijo. But I miss the fights. Is that terrible?
No, it isn’t. I miss them too.
The man at the market, Carmen. What did he say to you?
That the tomatoes looked lovely. You never say lovely, Steve. Not once in four years.
I thought you were finally getting better.
What did you bring us, Carmen?
Chicken tinga. Rafa made it, so it is too sweet. He is still in love.
With the girl from the bakery counter?
Now he brings home day-old bread every night. We are drowning in bread.
Cold out there this morning, Dale?
Eleven degrees at eight o’clock. Wind from the west at nine knots.
I only meant, is it cold.
It is within the normal range for October.
You still bring letters for my parents, Dale.
Every item goes to its address. That is the procedure.
They’ve been gone for eighteen months.
The address has not changed, Mr. Mercer.

direction: after Carmen has gone, closing the door
text: You told me that chair copies the oldest memories first. And you got out at sixty-one percent.
I was at the station all morning, and Biscuit isn’t a witness. So you tell me. What could I ask you that the man at the market couldn’t answer?
Don’t tell me something sweet. Copies can be sweet. Don’t act strange. Grieving people act strange.
I called 911 on Sunday night, when people walked into the water. That was before the chair.
After midnight, the 911 line rings in my kitchen. My machine keeps every call. I haven’t played Sunday’s yet.

direction: after playing back the call on her kitchen machine
text: Word for word. Both hellos.

direction: relieved, leaning over her crossword, his elbow near her mug
text: Seven letters. Maritime... marmite?
No copy is that bad at this. And you’ve put coffee in my lap.
How do I know you’re you?
You don’t. Nobody scanned me halfway. So you check my paperwork, same as everyone else.
The chair never got as far as Sunday night. My 911 call was on June’s machine, word for word. Whoever Carmen saw at the market, it wasn’t me.
For a year I’ve kept a list. People who got better overnight. Thirty-one names.
Lyle’s on it. My own deputy. Fourteen years, and this summer he started filing his reports on time.
We do this fairly. Otherwise we’re just frightened people making a list.
Gus Albano. Thirty years of his grandmother’s recipes, and on Monday a new pastry in his window.
Mateo’s coaching book. Lyle missed every game last spring. From June eleventh, he signed in at every one.
Walt moved to Washington in April. His signature is on a permit here, dated a day he was testifying in Washington.
Two I could take to a judge. And if I do, what do I tell Lyle’s boys? Mateo says they’ve never been happier.
Is Mrs. Penhallow on it? She was on the beach at midnight on Sunday.
Agnes? She hasn’t changed in forty years. She still corrects my grammar.
June’s list has thirty-one names, and most of them are feelings. Two are records: Lyle’s sign-in book and Walt Prior’s permit. Mrs. Penhallow isn’t on it.

direction: at the front door with the mail, saluting the sleeping beagle
text: Good morning, Officer Biscuit.
A most diligent animal. I will return at the scheduled interval.
She’s asleep, Dale. That is her schedule.
On Monday the post office told me Dale had already brought your letters here. Before I’d called them. So I asked for the paperwork.
At ten past six on Monday, I radioed the station to say you were here. Lyle was starting his shift. He answered.
Dale’s bag left the post office at four minutes past eight, with your letters already bundled for my house.
I didn’t phone the post office until twelve past eight. And Carmen only heard from Nora at lunch.
He had my mail sorted for your house before anyone told the post office I was here.
Lyle took my call at ten past six.
Then nobody tells Lyle where we go next. Or Dale.
Dale had my letters bundled for June’s house at 08:04. The post office didn’t know until 08:12. The only other person who knew was Lyle, who took June’s call at ten past six. They talk to each other.
June believes me. That makes one person.
Somebody with my face was at the market this morning. Lyle passes things to Dale. And two names on June’s list have paper behind them.
Paper is harder to replace than people. And June has keys to the Town Hall archive.
Town Hall closes at five. I have keys.
Then let’s find out which of them got better, and which of them got replaced.
Town Hall, after five. June had the keys, and I had a phone call to make.
I asked Tomás for help. It was the first time in a year I’d asked anybody for anything.
Three years of recordings. Original timestamps. You can stop calling it a hobby now.
I’ll start with thank you.
Nora says you broke into her aquarium.
I did.
...Cool. Why?
When I can prove it, you’re the first person I tell.
How many listeners does the podcast have now?
Fourteen. Mamá found the app, and now she leaves comments.
Every episode, the same comment. Eat something, mijo.
She’s not wrong, you know, Tomás.
Has Nora texted you lately?
Last night. No capitals, no apostrophes, same as always.
She just wrote, eat something. She sounds like Mamá now. That’s new.
Do you know how many boxes are down here?

Copies far from the bay stay in step on hold. Saren wants Mom’s notebook, and on Wednesday he wants the President.

Correctly delivered. Biscuit may inspect the chain of custody.

Twenty-three across, where it crosses eight down. Only the woman in cell two will see that square.

The June in cell two had my crossword in her hand: the M where 23 Across crosses 8 Down. The June on the radio guessed a T, so she has never been near that cell. Iris was right. By 4:02 June was out, and we were in the records room, waiting for the shift change at the back door.
Sheriff. Steve. I’m supposed to stop you.
Ben’s a tree in the school play this afternoon. He’s been practicing being a tree for a month.
Lyle. Your relief has signed.

Lyle’s copy could still make Ben’s play: Bus A at 4:29, at the school by 4:38. He chose the front row over his orders, and let us go.
June is out of her cell, and her copy is out at the north jetty, looking for me. Pell chose a beagle over his orders. Lyle’s copy chose a school play.
Five fugitives and a beagle. We needed a car nobody would look for.

text: Take the van. I don’t know why, but I trust you.

I can move my hand. That’s a start.
If this is a hospital, I’m changing hospitals.
Names first. Complaints after we have a plan.
How are you feeling, Dale?
Cold, stiff and starving. If this is a hospital, the food is terrible.
There isn’t any food here, Dale.
That is exactly my point, Nora.
Who is feeding June Calder’s beagle? I carry biscuits in my bag for her every morning.

Somebody had better be. She sulks at anyone who forgets.
Left at the pipes, right at the cold one, straight past the humming wall.

Mail carriers never forget a route, Nora. We only forget birthdays.
My boys have a game on Saturday. I’ve missed most of their games this year.
Then you’ll make the next one, Lyle.
Every single one, when I get out of here. I swear it.

I think somebody probably is, Lyle.
Then I hope he’s nicer to Steve Mercer than I was.
Boots. Then the pump. Then the far door. Again and again.

Wait. Now. Keep low. We can argue about my tone after we’re out.
The guard’s lap is twelve counts. On the next lap the far door shuts at 20 and the boots come back at 26. Four counts to cross. We can move.
Everybody’s good at something. Even Dale.
That hatch sticks. I’ve wedged it open twice already tonight.
Thirty years on a mail route. I could walk this one with my eyes shut.
I can keep that latch from catching.
I’ll remember the turns.
Good. I’ll handle the pump.
Lyle keeps the hatch from catching. Dale remembers every turn. I take the pumps. Water is the one thing on this ship I understand.
Three service branches. Let’s see what each one does.
The top dial reads an empty wash line. Ignore it. Watch the return and the bed flow.
Bed flow has to stay at three or more. The return has to drop below three.
Pressure down. Nobody’s breathing changes. That’s our route.
The Blue branch keeps the beds at 4 and drops the RETURN to 2. The hatch can open, and nobody’s breathing changes.
If he comes. When he comes. He’ll come.
Steve, if you ever hear this message: I am furious with you. I love you. Please stop making me do both alone.
My message for Steve is in Slot B, by my bed. It will wait for him.
I know every name in my row now. I have a route, a crew and a pump that behaves.
The hardest part is the waiting. I have never waited quietly for anything. Between patrols I lie still and think about a man who went quiet for eighteen months.
Helen. Frank. Steve is going to be so glad.
Mrs. Penhallow? Row three. I should remember that.
And you, under the frost... you can hear me, can’t you?
Under the frost, something opened one enormous eye. It looked at me. Then it closed again.
Sentinel Point. An old antenna field in the fog north of town, flags on every mast, and the President of the United States due at noon.
We spent Tuesday in the back room of Gus’s bakery, planning on flour sacks.
We couldn’t call anyone. The FBI’s man at the signing was Rook’s copy, and Rook’s list had names in Washington.
So we used what we had. Halcyon runs the sound for the signing, Stephen still has their crew pass, and Dad’s tape has the tone.
June wrote to the President in her own hand. Pell would deliver it the way he delivers everything: into the right hand, on time.
Gus had two catering passes for the press tent. June and Iris would use them at the red window, at ten past eleven, on foot, in his aprons and hairnets, carrying croissants.
Can you see the trucks from here? I can barely see my own feet.
Good. Fog is very flattering. Nobody looks like a wanted poster in fog.
Dad used to say fog makes every sound feel closer.
He said it on the boat, every summer. I remember that one. I think I do.
I had two croissants from Gus this morning. He gave me a third one for free.
He thinks you’re me, Stephen. My face is on every poster.
He said the poster doesn’t do me justice. He’s right, you know.
Rook’s copy wished you luck finding me.
I told him the truth. You’re very close. You’re under the sound desk.
Please stop enjoying this so much.
I can’t. This is the most fun I’ve had in my whole short life.
Who is looking after Biscuit today?
The Sheriff’s neighbor. I left written instructions. Four pages, with diagrams.
Four pages, for one beagle?
She is a very important beagle. She has a schedule.
Dale’s route has two hundred and twelve mailboxes. I know every one of them.

I like the dogs, and the people who say thank you. Mostly the dogs.
The coffee in the press tent is terrible. I’ve had four cups.
You don’t seem to mind it very much.
Rook takes his coffee black. I keep putting sugar in mine. I don’t know why.
Do you ever think about him? The one you were made from?
Every single day. He snores, apparently.
I wonder if mine dreams. Down there, in the cold.
This truck is older than you are. I rewired half of it myself.
It still sounds good, though.
Of course it does. I have good ears too. Mine are just older.
Before this, I built explosions for the movies. Six films, and never one real fire.
And now you run sound checks in the fog?
The government pays worse. But the sandwiches are better.
Crew credentials. Loyal asset. Very important face.
My face is on every poster in the county. So is yours.
Then one of us should hide. I vote you.
The gate card has three windows. Red at 11:10 is for deliveries on foot. No vehicles at all.
Gold at 11:50 is for the signers. The President’s guards search every vehicle with dogs.
Blue at 11:30 is for crew trucks. The guard scans the driver’s pass. If it shows green, the truck rolls through.
And I have no pass at all. So the guard can’t be allowed to see me.

direction: at the gate, holding up a wanted poster
text: You look like this poster.
I get that a lot. Scan me.
Saren’s hunter. Any luck?
He’s very close. I can feel it.
I’m expected. I’m usually expected everywhere.
Blue window, 11:30. Stephen drove, his pass scanned green, and I rode under the sound desk. Rook’s copy waved us through and wished Stephen luck finding me.
Registered mail for the President. Delivery cannot be delayed.
Registered mail goes into the addressee’s own hand. Nobody else may sign for her.

President Ward. Your letter. On time.
An increasingly rare achievement.

Sound check. I’m supposed to be under the desk.

The camera monitor shows the click the moment it leaves this desk.
The stage van shows the television feed. That runs two seconds late, because of the satellite.
Half a second. Good ears. Who taught you?
My dad.
Sound covers 170 meters in half a second. The fence-line strip in the Halcyon truck shows the click at 0.5 s, so the fence hears the desk. Every speaker on the site is mine.
We were in. Stephen as a loyal asset, Pell as the mail, and me at the sound desk with Dad’s tape of the ninth-night tone.
Ward signed for Pell’s letter at 11:54, with a fresh bandage on her left wrist. The public ceremony starts at 11:58.
June and Iris were already inside, in hairnets, somewhere near the service tunnel. Iris knew the crew’s routes. She used to walk them.
If they swap her, it happens between the hatch and the podium.
So we watch the hatch. I’m very good at being looked at.
In the fog between the antennas, an old woman was walking a dog. Mrs. Penhallow. Miles from her pier, again.
Every ninth night, when the bay sounds that tone, every copy near Bellwether walks to the water. Dad taped it.
If it played on every speaker at once, every copy on the site would answer it at once. In front of everybody.
At ten to twelve, the earpiece in Stephen’s hand stopped asking him for reports. It asked for me, by name.

What’s Tirel?
He didn’t answer.
What did the press ask you?
My favorite food. I said Sunday dinner at La Marea. Then I wasn’t sure whose memory that was.
It belongs to both of us. It was a good answer.
My hands are shaking. Are yours shaking too?
They’ve been shaking since six this morning.
Good. I was worried it was only me.
The last time I sat at a desk out here, four generals stood behind me.
Were they as nervous as I am?
Less. Breathe, Mercer. The tape won’t play any faster if you hold your breath.
Your father’s tape is in good shape. Who stored it?
He did. Cool and dry, and labeled in pencil. He labeled everything.
Then I would have hired him in a heartbeat.
Iris is right beside me. She’s counting her steps out loud.
Is she all right down there?
She says she’s fine. She says it the way you always do.
I just gave the press a short interview. They loved me. Now, four feeds and one President. Possibly two.
Iris said Ward’s own doctor scanned her weeks ago. A copy made back then can’t know about this morning.
And this morning she burned her left wrist on the folder. Pell wrote it down. Left wrist, bandaged.
Podium camera. The woman at the lectern just waved. Her left wrist is bare.
Stair camera. The doctor is helping a patient down the east stair. Her left wrist is bandaged.

Service tunnel, east stairs. The doctor has the real President.
We’re on it.

Dad’s tape. Cued, and ready.

Blue reaches the lectern, the back fence and the service steps.

The tone goes out on Blue: the lectern, the back fence and the service steps, but not the press van. June’s reply comes back on Slate, to Stephen and me alone.
Service tunnel. We see them. Give us a few seconds.
The team gets to the patient at 11:58 and fourteen seconds. Not one second sooner.
The speakers switch to the anthem at eighteen seconds past. Your tone runs two seconds. It has to finish before then.
Fourteen people stopped in the fog and turned toward the sea.
Fourteen. Rook. The physician. The woman at the microphone.
We have President Ward.
She has my letter. She read it by flashlight in the tunnel, and she believes us. She wants to meet the man at the sound desk.
At 11:58:15 Dad’s tone went out on every site speaker. Fourteen people stopped and turned toward the sea, the woman at the microphone among them. June and Iris had the real President.
Fourteen copies turned toward the sea at once, in front of everyone who mattered. The real President was in a service tunnel, with a bandaged wrist and June Calder.
Iris told me later that the tone pulled at her too. She held on to June’s sleeve and counted Sunday dinners until it passed.
Rook’s copy slipped away into the fog. Before he went, he asked me one thing.
Is he awake? The other one?
An hour later, in a locked room under the array, the President of the United States thanked me.
Thank you, Mr. Mercer. Their Prefect wants one thing from us by the ninth night. Our space-fold engine.

Asleep under the bay. Can you read it?
This page... Madam President. He should hear it from us.
Now we owe you an explanation.

Your mother’s shorthand. Sentinel Point, nine years ago. I was in that room.
We are prepared to discuss the practical status of our demonstration.
After you explain the difference between practical and actual.
Coffee, General? It comes from the machine in the hall.
Is it any good, Mrs. Mercer?
No. But it is hot, and it doesn’t pretend to be anything else.

My husband is a ham. He talked about it at dinner for a week.
Then I hope your husband enjoyed the show.
Your building has no windows, Mrs. Mercer. And no tea.
I brought my own. Jasmine. There is enough for two.
Then this meeting has already gone better than I expected.

My card had two words he might use. One meant a technical demonstration. The other meant a performance, as on a stage.

He proposes comparing our performances.
Performances. Yes. That is... a fair word.
That would be a useful place to begin.
He said biaoyan, a performance, as on a stage. I translated it exactly and noted that he chose it. The American heard the word and did not argue.
Both men were waiting for the other to blink. Somebody had to ask the first question, and it had to be me.
Our observers saw a ring of light on your screen. We were never allowed inside your room.
Our observers saw a ring of light on yours. We never went inside your room either.
Each man could only speak for his own machine. And the joint minutes would be read by the whole world.
There was no space-fold engine.
There was no engine at our test either.
Then we can discuss what to do next.
Each delegate described his own machine, and neither had an engine. In the joint minutes we wrote only what both sides saw: a ring of light.
Both demonstrations were staged. Both sides admitted it, in this room, to each other. Then they agreed to keep lying, together.
Dates. Names. What each person actually said. Someone may need the truth one day.
When they understood that they had bluffed each other, the whole room laughed. Tired laughter. The kind that lets you breathe.
Everyone agreed to keep lying. It may be the most honest thing I have seen.
Shaw took us into the Meridian laboratory. It was a film set. The doors were painted on the walls.

Your mother wrote ‘heard this before’ beside a drum beat that isn’t there. I want to know where she heard it.
Mine had a better explosion.

Mine fooled four generals.
Mine fooled six. And a premier.
You knew my mother nine years ago. What was she like in that room?
Tired, like all of us. But she brought a tin of lemon cookies and shared them with both sides.
Nobody refuses a cookie from the interpreter. It was very clever of her.
I walked here from the hotel. An old woman with a dog said good morning to me in Mandarin.
In Mandarin? Out here in Bellwether?
Perfect Mandarin. Then she asked me if I needed any bait.
How long have you two known each other?
Nine years. We were enemies for one week and friends ever since.
She still owes me a dinner. She lost a bet about the fog machine.
Are those really washing-machine drums?
Six of them, from a laundromat in Reno. The owner thought I was starting a business.
In a way, I was.
Thirty years of explosions, and I can still hear a mouse cough in the next room.
So can I. It makes the cinema very hard.
Sit in the back row. Nobody coughs in the back row.
Help me put her pages back in order.
This scrap is the American test. Two drum strikes, a missing beat, then a lamp flare.

And the minutes of the meeting at one table quote both tests. Your mother was in that room.
They heard the demonstrations nine years ago. They came here three years ago. We called them without knowing anyone was listening.
Heard this before. Mom heard that missing beat in the bay. In Dad’s reels.

Film log’s on the clipboard. Tell me what you see.
Drums, lamps and fog. If two effects hit on the very same frames, one cue can drive them both.
Ignore anything marked rehearsal. That was me testing bulbs.
Those drums survived six films and a congressional visit. They can manage one more show.
They fell for a show once. So we put on another one. Live, this time.
The drums and lamps hit together on frames 120, 128 and 136; the fog just drifts. One cue drives the whole effect. Shaw’s reactor can play again, and this time we play it live.
Beside it she wrote: “From Frank’s tapes. I cannot read it, but I know a language when I hear one.”
Three strokes. The second joins the first and climbs higher. Then a gap. Then a long stroke, lower than both.
Dad wrote the pitch on every reel. A higher number means a higher note.
I can read Helen’s shorthand. This is something else.
Then we keep listening.

Mom’s last page is Dad’s Reel 11: two joined tones rising, 220 to 330, a half-second gap, then a long 165, lower than both. Her margin says it repeats after the low note. It’s a language, and nobody on Earth can read it.
Two countries faked two tests and broadcast them on open radio. Something out there was listening, and it came. Mom heard the proof in the bay.
Shaw’s reactor still works, if one cue drives the drums and lamps. And Mom’s last page is a language from Dad’s tapes that nobody can read.
Mrs. Penhallow was standing by the reactor. Nobody had seen her come in.
A lie is only shameful when it’s lazy, Steven.
Smart woman. Who is she?
When I turned round, she was gone.

direction: from every screen and radio in the county
text: Midnight tomorrow, Madam President. The ninth night. The engine, or the scan resumes.
And Mr. Mercer. Come down to the beach at dawn. Alone.
Dawn on the beach. Saren came alone, the way he said he would: taller than the doorframes on his ship, and perfectly still.
Give me the notebook. Helen and Frank will walk out of the sea tomorrow morning.

direction: barely audible, to himself

I need a moment.
Your mother would like a word.

direction: from a small device in Saren’s hand; a splice, made by editing recording.voicemail
text: Come out with us, kiddo. Tonight.

direction: taking Dad’s recorder out of his cardigan pocket
text: I know every breath of her voicemail. Let me play it right next to this.
Same breath before ‘kiddo’. And a hole where four words used to be.
Saren’s message is Mom’s voicemail, cut and stitched: the same breath before ‘kiddo’, and a gap where ‘The bay is singing’ used to be. He has no message from her. He has my tape.
That’s my voicemail. You cut my mother out of her own message. No. You don’t get to trade the whole town for my family.
I kept the notebook. Saren had a promise, my mother’s voice cut to fit it, and nothing else.
Saren offered me my parents for Mom’s notebook. His proof was my own voicemail, cut to say what he wanted.
I said no. And for the first time I wondered how many times he’d done this before.
How many families on Tirel got a message like that?
He was quiet for a long time.
You should consider your parents.
I am. And everyone else’s.
Back at Sentinel Point, I told them the plan. It had a lot of holes. Shaw filled most of them with gaffer tape.
You are a terrible liar.
I know. That is why it has to be a show.
Before you decide. Every sleeper you wake cuts one of us loose, and that one starts to forget. Stephen too.
Then it isn’t my decision alone.
Wake them. Even if we start forgetting. I vote to do it.
Seconded. I’ll write things on my hand.
Here’s the show. We stage the test again, live, so nothing ever repeats. And while they’re watching it, we wake everyone.
Did you water the balcony flowers before we left?
This morning. The irises have two new buds. I counted them.

Carmen called. She asked if we’re coming on Sunday. I told her yes, both of us.
Both of us meaning you and me? Or Nora and me?
Nora and you. I’ll be happy just to help set the plates.
What have you lost so far?
Small things. The name of Nora’s first goldfish. The way to her old school.
It doesn’t hurt. It’s like a radio station drifting slowly out of range.
I’m so sorry, Iris. Truly.
I’m writing a list on my hand. Steve, Mom, Dad, Biscuit.
Biscuit made your list before the rest of the town?
Biscuit is very important. Ask Pell.
When this is over, I’d like to do one show at the radio station. Just one.
The machine has my old chair now.
Then we take it back together. You do the sound. I’ll do the talking.
I’ve used eleven rolls of gaffer tape today. That’s a personal record.
Is that good news or bad news?
In my business, it means the show is nearly ready.
I called my daughter last night. She asked what I’m building this time.
What did you tell her?
A very honest lie. She said that sounded exactly like me.
How’s your wrist, Madam President?
Bandaged and famous. Half the country has seen it on television.
My doctor wants to look at it. I said, not you, thank you.
A week ago I had never heard of Bellwether. Now I won’t forget it.
Try Sunday dinner at La Marea before you leave. Carmen will feed you twice.
If we’re all still here on Sunday, I’ll book a table.
Three feeds, three jacks. Shaw, give me a cue.
One jack carries my lamp tester. It flashes on beat five, every time.
One carries my rehearsal film, looping on beat four. And one is my own hand on the button.
Shaw cued beat four, then beat seven. Birch flashed on five both times. Ash flashed on four both times.
Elm flashed on four, then on seven. It followed her.
Their old test failed because it repeated. Ours won’t. Every answer will be live.
Birch is Wen’s fixed tester, stuck on beat 5. Ash is Shaw’s rehearsal loop, stuck on 4. Elm follows Shaw’s hand, live. Only Elm can answer a cue nobody has seen before.
I ran a paper trial. Three receipts. Only one of them would convince me, if I were them.
The dock receipt says a camera saw the lamps. The mast receipt says the ship measured them. The shore receipt says the ship got our crew’s numbers.
The fleet trusts nothing that its own ship did not measure.
My crew pass still opens the antenna passage. I checked. Twice.
And the sleepers are in the Gallery. Mom and Dad are in row nine.
The ship must measure the event.
Then we take the rig to its antenna.

direction: on Frank’s radio, a channel he thinks is private
text: Prefect, they’re at the Sentinel Point workshop. All of them. They’re building something.
The fleet only trusts what its own ship measures, so the show has to go in through the ship’s antenna. Stephen’s pass opens the antenna passage. The rest of us go to the Gallery and wake everyone.
Three couplers, identical plugs. I’d like the one that works.
I tested all three twice. Once to see the cue go out, and once to hear what leaks back.
We need a signal going out and nothing coming back. Otherwise the ship hears my theater.
Careful. A dead coupler also lets nothing back. It looks perfect until you check the cue.
I can carry this. You get them awake.
Both delegations are at your disposal, Mr. Mercer.
Coupler A leaks the stage hum, B passes nothing, and C passes Shaw’s cue with a clean return. Stephen carries C to the antenna.
The plan: Shaw and Wen stage the Meridian test again, live, on Elm through coupler C. Stephen carries the rig into the ship’s antenna, so the ship measures the show for itself.
The rest of us go to the Gallery and wake everyone, Mom and Dad included. Iris and Stephen voted for it, knowing what it costs them.
Dad’s name. I know it. I just...
Frank.
Frank. I’ll write it on my hand.
That night we went back under the bay, through the aquarium tunnel. Pell stayed behind with Biscuit. Ten minutes later he caught up with us, carrying her.
The third ninth night. We came in through the intake tunnel, soaked to the knees.
Unscheduled visitors detected. Would you like to be scanned while you wait?
We’ve done this one. It ends with a flood.
I’ll take your word for it. I wasn’t conscious for the good part.
Steve? They put me back under after the pump trick. Five months. And thirteen months before that, when you barely said a word.
I’m so glad to hear you angry.
I can break the link. Let me do this.
Did my mother notice? That it wasn’t me at her table?
She said you’d stopped arguing with her. That’s how she knew something was wrong.
Good. I’m going to argue with her all week.
Is anybody feeding Admiral properly? He gets sulky.
He stole my sandwich on the pier. Rye bread.
He hates rye. He was making a point.
He came to my whistle, Nor. Not hers. That’s when I started to wonder.
I know half this hall by name now. It’s like a very cold party.
Who is the best company down here?
Dale Kittredge. He says he’s never been this late with the mail in thirty years.
You wore my favorite coat for five months.
It is a good coat. I sewed the top button back on.
I’ve been meaning to do that for two years.
I know. I remembered meaning to.
I keep reaching for things she knows. Some of them are already gone.
Do you want me to stop asking you things?
No. Keep asking. I want to find out which answers are mine.
Is the name still there?
Frank. Dad. I check it every few minutes. I hate that I have to.
Then I’ll check it with you. Every few minutes.
I took this slip from a sleeping man in a very nice suit.
Is that strictly legal, Sheriff Calder?
I’ll write myself a ticket when we get home.
Adrian Rook is somewhere in this hall. The real one.
We’ll find him, June. I promise.
Good. He still owes me a coffee from twenty years ago.
Would you like to be scanned while you wait?
Still no, thank you. Very kind of you to ask again.
Your answer has been noted. The offer remains open.
It’s dropping, Iris. Fast.
These memories were borrowed. The choice is mine.
I can move. I can finally move.
Iris opened the release herself, watching her own memory drain. Nora can move.
I was afraid that if I wanted something, I would lose it too. That doesn’t excuse leaving you alone.
Then keep talking. We have a lot to do.
I laughed. I couldn’t help it. Then she laughed too.
I told Nora the truth about the thirteen months: I was afraid that if I wanted something, I’d lose it too. She told me to keep talking.
One door, one pass, one very important face. Let’s go.
This visitor slip gets me onto the observation deck. It won’t open a single door.
The lamp for the inner door is round the bend. You can only see it from the deck.
And I stay right here by Nora’s bed. I promised her.
Then I don’t walk on until somebody sees that lamp light up.
Calder saw the lamp. I’m heading up to the antenna. Don’t wait for me.
Stephen’s pass opened the inner pad. June saw the lamp light from the deck and called it in, and Stephen went on alone to the antenna with the rig. I stayed where I promised.
Nora is free. Iris paid for it with her own memory, and chose to.
Stephen is on his way to the antenna with the rig. Mom and Dad are somewhere in this hall, in row nine.
The ring. Where is it?
Sock drawer. I was afraid.
I left you something. Slot B. Press play.

direction: from every speaker in the Gallery at once
text: Steve, if you ever hear this message: I am furious with you. I love you. Please stop making me do both alone.
I think everyone heard that.
Good. Witnesses.
Nora and Iris looked at each other. Neither of them knew what to say.
Row nine. Mom and Dad, side by side, the way they always slept. I’d brought every sound I had.
We’ve kept the service route open. Tell me who to wake first.
I brought the sounds. I think they can hear us.
We kept this aisle open with a mop handle and a lot of shouting.
All that shouting? I can believe that.
Mostly mine. Dale helped. He shouts like a man who has met a lot of dogs.
Your mother just asked me if I’m eating enough. On a spaceship.
That’s how she says I love you.
I know. My mother does the exact same thing with soup.
How long were we under, kiddo?
Eighteen months, Dad. A year and a half.
That’s a lot of Thursdays. The club must think I quit.
They don’t. I called them on your radio. Gull nearly cried.
Did the boat make it back?
It drifted in the next morning. Your radio was still on.
Good radio. I told your mother it was a good radio.
You never told me the words, Mom.
There weren’t any, Steven. I made up the tune your first night home from the hospital.
The ship has been humming it for months.
Then the ship has good taste.
Is that Nora? She looks so tired.
She ran this whole hall while you were asleep, Mom.
Then she has earned a proper dinner. I’ll talk to Carmen.
He asked about his pajamas before he asked about me.
He’s awake, June. That’s what matters.
I know. I’m still telling everyone at the office.
Where are my clothes? Who has been wearing my clothes?
A man with your face, Adrian. He had your manners too, mostly.
Then he owes me a dry cleaning bill.
Dad. It’s Steve.
Nothing. He used to say a call sign is a name you can hear through static.
There are three call cards in his tray. They all look almost the same.
Dad’s call sign is on his old cassette, in Morse. But the tape is scratched. It always loses the very last letter.
K7BLW receiving. Helen? Steve?
Right here, Dad.
Dad’s card is K7BLW. The scratched cassette lost the last letter, the W: dot, dash, dash. I sent it again, and Dad answered his own call sign.
Your mother. Play her the song, kiddo. I’ll write it down for you.
That’s the song in the hum. All this time, the ship was humming Mom’s lullaby.
It starts at home. Up once, then up again. Back down to the middle note, then home, and hold it.
You used to sing this when I couldn’t sleep. Now I need you to wake up.
Steven. Oh, my boy.
Home, up, higher, back to the middle, then home and hold. Mom’s lullaby, the one the ship’s hum kept almost playing. She woke up singing the last note.
Adrian. It’s June. Come back to work.
June? Why am I in pajamas?
No recording this time. June talked to him, and the real Adrian Rook woke up asking about his pajamas.
Mrs. Penhallow? She taught half this town. She’s squinting at me like I spelled something wrong.
Her glasses case still has a price sticker from her bait shop. That one is hers.
The row list says the sleeper marked OT is on her left, and MV is on her right.
My glasses. Has somebody changed the price of bait while I was gone?
Who has been minding my bait stall, Steven?
I thought you had, Mrs. Penhallow. Every Sunday on the pier.
On Sundays? I never open on Sundays. Sunday is for church and the crossword.
Mrs. Penhallow’s glasses, from the middle tray. Her bed tag says she’s been asleep in here for three years. So who has been selling me bait?
Dad woke to his call sign, Mom to her lullaby, Adrian Rook to June’s voice, and Mrs. Penhallow to her reading glasses.
Somewhere above us, Rook’s copy was losing the man he’d been pretending to be. And he was telling Saren everything he had left.
I’m forgetting. Prefect, they’re at the antenna. They have a rig.
Take Stephen. Break the apparatus. Bring me the original.
They took the rig off Stephen and broke it over the rail. Then they took me.
We will finish your scan. This time there will be no interruption.

direction: strapped into the scan chair, frightened
text: The chair pulled at everything I knew. My dad’s name. It was... it’s on Stephen’s hand. Why is it on his hand?
Stop.
Four thousand years of unchanged records. Three hundred and twelve human lives. Show us one record that changed, and we will choose.
Three hundred people just woke up in wet pajamas.
And not one of them has shoes.
I’m starting a line for blankets. Somebody has to.
You kept a list, kiddo. Dates and everything.
You taught me. Put a date on everything.
I did, didn’t I? Good. I’m glad something stuck.
It sings in phrases, like a person thinking out loud.
Can you understand what it says?
Not every word. But I can hear when it means something.
Every door on this ship just opened at once.
Is everybody all right down there?
Dale Kittredge is asking for his mailbag. So yes, I think so.
You want a record that changed? I’ve been keeping a list.
Nora’s good morning, on Saturday and on Sunday. The same breath, the same pause, both days.
Rook telling June to sit tight. The same take on her voicemail and through a door in the mountains.
And Iris, on Monday. She said the same words twice, and the second time she paused somewhere new.
Same voice. In October she played back a recording. On Monday she chose her own words.
We remember birthdays, quarrels, songs and the things people tried again. Open the doors. Wake them.

Nora’s good morning and Rook’s line were recordings, played back. Iris chose her words twice, differently. The same voice that once replayed Nora now speaks for itself. The Choir heard a record change, and chose.
The frost broke. Something tall sat up in Row Zero for the first time in three hundred years. It looked at Mom, and it bowed.
Row Zero holds one who is not human. We took it from Tirel. We call it Wick. It has not stopped dreaming.
That’s the one under the frost. It hums when you talk to it.
That’s the phrase from your father’s tapes. Two joined notes going up, a little gap, then one long low note.
I wrote it in my margin, Steven. After the low note, it starts all over again.
I heard you in the hum. The Choir was dreaming with you.
Tirel hid. All seven worlds hid. They watched you erase yourselves and were afraid you would erase them.
Page 12: two joined strokes rising, a gap, one long low stroke, and then it starts again. Mom followed Wick from phrase to phrase. Tirel was never destroyed. It hid. They all hid.
We wanted your ears, kiddo. We always liked having the rest of you along too.
I thought saying no was the worst thing I’d ever done.
Dad’s note from the boat: they wanted my ears, and they always liked having the rest of me along too. For eighteen months I thought saying no was the worst thing I’d ever done.
The Choir chose. Every door on the ship opened, and three hundred people woke up at once in wet pajamas. The crew had no procedure for it.
Tirel hid. All seven worlds hid. The Veyri have spent nine hundred years afraid of neighbors who were afraid of them.
You’d have been the third person in the Gallery, kiddo. Then who would have come for us?
I should have told you what we were doing.
We’re here now. All of us.
Something enormous just came out of the sky. We have one hour.
The Vigil. It followed us here in silence, to check the Prefect’s word. His report goes out in one hour.
The rig was in pieces. And all over town, the copies had begun to forget.
One hour. The rig was in pieces, and all over town the copies were forgetting.
Then I remembered Halcyon’s tower. Every ninth night for a year it had talked to the ship, alone.
The rig is in pieces. We need another way onto their antenna.
We don’t need the rig. KBWR’s tower already talks to the ship.
Good morning! Up next, another hour of uninterrupted favorites.
Rick, buddy. I need my microphone back.
Your request is important to us!
Has anybody got dry socks? I’ll trade a perfectly good vacuum tube.
There’s a lost and found behind the coffee machine.
Then I’m saving the world in somebody’s bowling socks.
I wired half this booth, you know. Labeled every cable.
Somebody took the labels off when the new owners came.
Then I’ll put them back. Every single one. After breakfast.
Is there coffee? I remember liking coffee.
You do. Black and very strong, two cups before breakfast.
Good. That one is still mine. I’m keeping it.
Do we both talk on air, or do we take turns?
Take turns. People will think the radio is broken.
People already think that. I listened to your replacement for a week.
Good morning, Rick. How are you feeling today?
I am excellent! It is currently yesterday!
That sounds about right, buddy.
When I was a girl, our village had one loudspeaker on a pole.
What did the loudspeaker play all day?
Weather, news and my aunt’s opinions. Mostly my aunt’s opinions.
Rick keeps a log of everything. Including the last time a human got the microphone.
Three slips. My station ident, a traffic report and a news bulletin.
The ident never stops the music. Traffic waits until the song ends. A bulletin puts a person on the air.
And yesterday’s forecast was sunny!
Thank you, Rick. We’re live now.
06:01 was the ident, 06:03 the traffic and 06:05 the bulletin, the one that hands the air to a human. I signed the bulletin as duty host, and KBWR was mine again.
Same labels as the rig. You remember which is which, I hope.
Birch was your fixed tester. Ash was the old rehearsal loop. Elm followed Shaw’s hand.
Returns: A is the booth echo, B is a shore camera, and C is measured aboard their ship.
The route was here the whole time. It’s why they bought the station.
Elm follows Shaw’s hand, live, the way it did at the rig. Return C is a measurement signed aboard the Long Patience, the only kind the fleet trusts. Elm into Return C.
K7BLW calling the Thursday club. We’re going to need a few more operators.
Yesterday I sent signal three. Today I’m sending signal four. Let’s see who keeps up.
The official channel just sent back three. That’s yesterday’s cue.
Gull here. Cedar and Marsh both say four. Marsh says the wind just turned west out at the Point.
Ask them both about the wind again, Gull.
Marsh says it’s dropping now. Cedar said the same words as last time, exactly.
Short messages. Repeat the cue number, then pass it on.
Understood. Sentinel Point, do you read?

The official line sent back yesterday’s cue. Cedar can repeat a cue but can’t see the field. Marsh, out past Sentinel Point, answered with a fresh wind reading. Marsh is our eyes, and Gull carries the cues down the coast.
KBWR is live again, and the tower that carried the ship’s signals for a year will carry ours: Elm into Return C.
Dad’s club is relaying the cues. Marsh at Sentinel Point, Gull down the coast, and then anyone on Earth with a radio.
Coast relay ready. They’re answering from everywhere, Frank.
Everywhere?
Every continent, kiddo. Hams never really switch off.
Carmen calls the restaurant list. Mateo calls the fire crews. Rafa calls everyone who owes him a favor.
That is a long list.
Listen to your local radio. Tonight, we need you to take part.
Mrs. Penhallow walked into the booth with her bait bucket. Nobody had told her where we were.
I brought something in my bucket.
Wind through the western towers. Last evening. Original take.
Mrs. Penhallow, I have never heard you say anything that wasn’t about bait.
I recorded it a long time ago, Steven. Before I had hands that smelled of herring.
You’re one of them. You’re the records officer Iris told me about.
Part of her. The part that stayed for the people.
Veyr was our home, Steven. Our sun failed. That is the last wind that ever blew through our city.
My mother has called forty people already. Thirty of them owe her money.
Wait. People actually owe Carmen money?
Tabs at the restaurant. She’s calling in every single one tonight.
Yesterday I was asleep under the bay. Today I’m running a town.
You were always running the town, Nor.
True. But now people are actually listening to me.
Iris called my brothers before I could. She knew every number by heart.
She’s had your phone for five months.
I want that phone back. And she rearranged all my apps.
I have called the bakery, the church and both bars. The bars were awake.
Thank you, Carmen. I mean it.
Thank me by eating something. You haven’t eaten since Thursday. I can tell.
She argued with me twice tonight already. Twice, Steve!
Is that a good thing?
It is the best night of my whole life.
You were a good student, Steven. Too loud. I liked that.
You weren’t really my teacher, were you?
She was. I learned her very carefully. I only kept her chair warm.
Why a bait stall, of all things?
Nobody buys bait, so nobody stays long. And I could watch the water all day.
My staff wanted a long speech. I told them to listen to local radio.
How is your wrist, Madam President?
Bandaged, and still mine. Thank you for that.
Nine years ago I would have unplugged her lamps.
You tried. And my fake fooled more generals than yours.
It did not. My test fooled two admirals as well.
I brought the fog machine. Just in case.
In case of what, exactly?
In case it needs to look impressive. It always needs to look impressive.
Two street captains, one spare phone and six thousand porch lights. Easy.
Pier can see Orchard’s porch lights from the harbor. Orchard faces the hills, so they can’t see Pier at all.
Both streets have the radio on. And Mateo wants one phone kept free for the fire crew.
Listen, repeat the cue, then switch. And leave a line free for anyone who needs help.
Nora set it up in ten minutes. Orchard starts on my cue, Pier answers what it sees, and the spare phone stays free for the fire crew.
Your timing is late.
Your lamps are dim.
Wonderful. You can both fix it while we’re on air.
Shaw calls the lamps when she sees the harbor answer, and Wen raises the grid on Shaw’s mark. Nine years of rivalry, one cue sheet.
There is a pencil mark after the last gust. I made it myself.
The fleet should hear home first. Then a voice answering them, live, that nobody recorded.
A recording can remind them of home. We’ll answer it with something happening now.
The Veyr wind plays through to Mrs. Penhallow’s pencil mark, after the last gust. Then the Choir’s return opens, live. Home as it was, then a voice answering them now.
Mrs. Penhallow is part of the ship’s record keeper, the part that stayed ashore with us. She brought me the last wind on Veyr in her bait bucket.
Every porch light in Bellwether is waiting for my cue. Shaw has the lamps, Wen has the grid, and the Choir will answer live.
Lamps up.
Grid up. Late, but up.
Bellwether, this is Steve Mercer, live. I can’t do this alone, and for once I’m not going to try.
I knocked over the microphone stand, caught it and kept going.
Steve. Who’s... Frank. Dad. It’s on my hand.
It’s on mine too. Stay with me.
Orchard is listening for you, Steve. The pier is watching Orchard.
Careful. Two Pier lamps are still on from the rehearsal. Don’t count those.
First street ready. Second street ready. Look at the harbor, Steve.
Field lights following. We can match that.
I called Orchard. When a fresh Pier flash answered Orchard’s change, I released Shaw’s lights. A reply, made live, that nobody could have recorded.
I logged all three faders, kiddo. One of them only looks connected.
With the coast plugged in, Reed and Bell both answered two beats late. With the coast unplugged, Reed went quiet.
Bell kept answering anyway. So Bell is only an echo inside the building.
The fourth signal goes out on beat forty. Shaw goes when the coast answers. Wen needs the next two beats.
And my power crew needs everything back by the start of beat forty-five.
Holding. Now, Wen.
Grid response confirmed. Both networks.
The far relay has you.
Reed went silent when the coast was unplugged, so Reed is the real coast return. Its reply landed at 42 for Shaw, and Wen took 43 and 44. Both grids answered, live.
Last cue. The wind on Veyr, and then the Choir. Nobody talks over them.
Mrs. Penhallow marked the last gust at fifty. It keeps ringing until fifty-two.
I confirm on beat fifty-one. Give me two beats to talk.
We are here. We have changed. Listen.
Keep the voices clear. Let them hear every one.
For the first time in nine hundred years, the fleet stopped to listen.
The wind on Veyr rang out through 52. At 53, with nobody else on the line, the Choir answered. Nothing repeated, because nothing was recorded.
Porch lights, field lamps, two national grids, a planet’s worth of radios and three hundred and twelve human voices. None of it recorded. All of it answering.
To the Vigil’s instruments, Earth had just tested an engine that could reach the fleet in an afternoon.
Saren is on the pier. He’s going for the tower.
Mr. Mercer. Turn it off, or I will come up that tower and finish your scan on air.
You’re on air now, Prefect. Your whole fleet is listening. Say that again.
The town stood on the pier in his way. June. The Reyes brothers. Carmen with a ladle. Pell with Biscuit. Stephen. And two hundred copies who had decided where they lived.
Then he can go through us.
Biscuit and I have chosen our route.
He’s sitting down. Mateo is sitting on him.
He says this is undignified.
And Admiral has stolen his command crystal. He thinks it’s a sandwich.
Take me back to the ship. I will not sign anything.
Mrs. Penhallow took the microphone out of my hand. Then she argued with herself, on the air, while the whole planet listened.
I will not confirm this report.
To do so would violate every record we have kept.
For a year I told you the engine was in a notebook, Saren. So you would keep looking, instead of telling the fleet there was nothing here to fear.
You have spent three years selling bait to people you like. Tell them what you learned.
Last winter the boats came in empty. I let every one of them pay me in spring.
You can spend another nine hundred years remembering home, or let someone make a new one.
I remember the wind. You remember the people.
My echo stood behind the bait counter last winter and let the boats pay in spring. I remember the wind. She remembers the people. I will let her win.
There is a sealed survey in the Prefect’s file. He told us every world was taken.
Three slips. Reef Six has water and air, and a beacon there answers every call.
Sound Four has air, but no water at all. Reach Two has water and air, and it was visited three times.
He found a home. He hid it because the mission would have ended.
Then finish the mission.
Reach 2: water, air and three separate surveys of empty ground. The Prefect found a home for the fleet and sealed it, because a home would have ended his mission.
Saren, you will remain yourself. You will have to remember being wrong.
I have no procedure for that.
Neither do I.
The danger, measured aboard our own ship. A home, surveyed empty three times. And three hundred and twelve people worth meeting. I have confirmed the report.
The report is confirmed. The fleet will measure an engine that does not exist, meet three hundred and twelve people, and learn of a home it was never told about.
I did not reconcile Saren. He will have to live with being wrong. So will I.
They are dangerous, and they sing. Go around.
Here are three hundred and twelve lives you should meet. And here is a world where we can live.
Wick is adding a message for Tirel.
The Vigil is turning.
And now, the forecast for yesterday: sunny, with a chance of spaceships!
The Vigil turned, and the fleet turned with it. At sunrise the Long Patience rose out of the bay, with Wick aboard. The whole coast watched it go. Somebody on the pier started to clap.
Your memories are yours now. You need no more re-syncs.
A face of my own. It will take getting used to.
Thank you for helping us. I haven’t forgiven the kidnapping.
Dinner is still at six.
I go back to the aquarium on Monday. The otter pups won’t remember me.
They’ll remember you. You’re the one who argues with the vet.
Everybody argues with the vet. I just win.
Somebody rearranged our kitchen. Everything is in alphabetical order.
That was Iris. She thought it looked tidy.
The forks are under F. I’m leaving them there. It makes me laugh every morning.
Admiral came to my whistle this morning. Straight out of the water.
Your second note went up again. I heard it from the pier.
It always went up, Steve. Somebody else was whistling it wrong.
I chose this face myself. It’s strange to be surprised by a mirror.
It suits you. It really does.
Nora says the nose is too serious. I think that means she likes it.
Carmen invited me to dinner on Sunday. Is that a trap?
With Carmen, dinner and a trap can be the same thing.
Then I’ll bring bread. Nora says bread is always safe.
Six o’clock, Steve. Both of you. All of you.
You mean Iris is invited too?
Iris too. She sat at my table for five months. Now she can help with the dishes.
I kept your plate warm every Sunday. This Monday I am not throwing it out.
You never had to keep it, Carmen.
I know. That is why I did.
Ben has the school play tonight. He wants both of us in the front row.
Two Lyle Boones in one front row.
The other one learned the lines with him. I’m still learning mine.
I still go to every game. Now we take turns driving.
He’s better at the snacks. I’m better at yelling at the umpire.
We’re working on that. Both of us.
Biscuit knows every porch on the route. I am still learning the gates.
The blue gate on Harbor Street sticks. Kick it low.
Kick it low. I have written that down.
First free morning in thirty years. No mailbag, and no frozen bed.
What are you going to do instead, Dale?
Sleep in a real bed. A warm one. Then go fishing.
Try it, Steve. It’s green, but it’s honest.
Gus, this is actually really good.
Don’t tell anyone. I have a reputation for plain bread.
She charges ten cents less than me for worms. On purpose.
Somebody kept this stall open for three years, Agnes.
And in three years, nobody bought a single worm.
The ship left without me, Steven. I asked it to.
